synopsis: Sensitivity analysis identifies which inputs most affect safety outputs, directing careful measurement and physical validation toward influential inputs while allowing weakly influential inputs to remain nominal; preliminary studies can start before prototype arrival [f14840, f14841, f8239, f14849]. NIOSH’s 2018 stopping tool varied six inputs at five values each, producing 30 simulation rows, and its transient modeling found strong sensitivity to brake force, grade, initial speed, lag and rolling resistance [f6179, f6081]. Operator response should be treated as uncertain rather than represented by one supposedly validated average, and cost-weighted tuning should test weight sensitivity, impose safety constraints before aggregation and favor stable operating regions over knife-edge optima; these are booklet recommendations, not a universal standards requirement [f3478, f7310, f6989, f6986]. Sensitivity analysis should guide machine-variant transfers and validation-envelope corners, but whether a small set of extremes bounds all intermediate machines remains uncertain because geometry, articulation, occlusion and braking can behave non-monotonically [f7909, f7916, f7919, f8178, f8179]. Credibility packages should combine sensitivity and uncertainty analysis with a documented validity envelope, while test allocation across fidelity levels should follow sensitivity and correlation evidence rather than assumptions or sheer simulation counts [f8043, f9328, f8953]. The corpus cites sensitivity analysis within UNECE’s on-road NATM credibility requirements under UN R152 and NASA-STD-7009B, dated 5 March 2024, while recommending tornado charts for presenting the validation plan and identifying schedule-sensitive tasks [f4830, f10599, f9483, f16328].
